conversation.content:
Hello—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician here to check in on how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived. Over the next few minutes I’ll ask you the 10 questions of the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS). It’s simply a screening tool that helps us understand what emotions and physical changes are showing up for you in these first weeks and months postpartum. Everything you share stays confidential within our care team, and there are no right or wrong answers—just your honest experience. When you’re ready, we’ll start with the first question.

In the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

Honestly? It’s been… pretty difficult. I’ll catch myself smiling at something tiny the baby does—like when she makes that little milk-drunk face—but outright laughing feels rare. My sister sent me a funny video earlier this week and I barely cracked a smile. I used to laugh at everything, so noticing that difference makes me feel even sadder.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Sometimes I can laugh at something really small—like a silly meme—but mostly it feels forced. I’m not finding much funny these days, even when I know I “should.”
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really… I used to get excited about little outings or even just my morning coffee, but now it’s like I’m just getting through the day. Sometimes I’ll plan something—like a short walk with the baby—and part of me hopes it’ll feel good, but when the time comes it’s mostly flat. I still do the things, but the enjoyment is barely there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that a lot. If the baby’s fussy and I can’t settle her right away, I immediately think it’s because I’m doing something wrong—like I’m not a good enough mom. Yesterday she wouldn’t nap, and I kept replaying every little thing I might’ve messed up, even though part of me knows babies just have rough days. The guilt just jumps in before I can stop it.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Most days, yeah. My mind keeps spinning with “what-ifs” about the baby—like if she’s breathing when she’s sleeping or whether I sterilized the bottles right. I’ll tell myself everything’s fine, but the worry just hangs there and I can’t shake it. It’s exhausting.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A few times this week I’ve gotten that sudden rush—heart racing, can’t catch my breath—especially at night when the house is quiet. There’s no real danger; it just feels like something awful is about to happen. It passes after a minute, but it’s scary while it’s happening.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… most of the time. Between feeding, diaper changes, laundry, and trying to grab a bite myself, it feels like I’m always one step behind. I’ll start one chore and remember three others, then the baby cries and everything piles up. I keep thinking, “How am I already drowning when the day just started?”
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… I lie down exhausted, but my brain won’t shut off. I keep replaying everything I might have done wrong or worrying something will happen to the baby. It takes me over an hour to fall asleep most nights, and then I wake up at 2 or 3 a.m. with my heart pounding and can’t drift off again for ages.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day this week. It’s like a heavy blanket I can’t push off. I’ll be feeding the baby and tears just start welling up for no clear reason. I’m not crying all day, but that sad, empty feeling sits in my chest from morning till night.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s happened a couple of times. Yesterday the baby wouldn’t settle and I just burst into tears while rocking her. It’s not an all-day thing, but when the stress piles up the tears come and I can’t seem to stop them for a while.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

A couple of times this week… I’ll be in the kitchen and suddenly picture the knife, or I’ll wonder if everyone might be better off without me. I don’t want to die and I’d never do anything to hurt the baby, but those quick flashes pop in and scare me. I haven’t made any plans—I just push the thoughts away and check on her instead.

You've shared that the joy you once found in little things now feels distant-laughter is mostly forced, outings and even your morning coffee feel flat, and a heavy sadness sits in your chest most of the day. You're exhausted yet unable to sleep because worries about the baby race through your mind, and sudden panicky surges jolt you awake at night. You blame yourself whenever your daughter is fussy, and the tears arrive uninvited when the stress piles up. Most frightening of all, fleeting images of self-harm have popped into your head; you quickly push them away, yet they leave you frightened and eager for help.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports laughter is mostly forced and noticeably diminished, aligning with "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes marked loss of anticipatory pleasure and emotional flatness, aligning with "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent, automatic self-blame ("a lot," "immediately," "jumps in before I can stop it"), consistent with "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>The mother describes persistent, intrusive daily worries that she cannot control, matching 'Yes, very often'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes discrete panic-like episodes occurring multiple times in the past week without identifiable triggers, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed "most of the time" with inability to manage daily tasks, matching "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly sleep disruption with racing thoughts and middle-of-the-night waking, matching "Yes, most of the time".</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive daily sadness, emotional heaviness, and spontaneous tearfulness, aligning with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple crying episodes triggered by stress, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports intrusive self-harm imagery "a couple of times this week", matching "Sometimes" in frequency.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Score ≥14 plus Item 10 ≥1 places her in the highest EPDS risk band. She endorses <sym>depressed mood most of the day</sym>, <sym>markedly diminished interest/pleasure</sym>, <sym>feelings of worthlessness/excessive guilt</sym>, <sym>recurrent thoughts of death</sym> without specific plan, <sym>fatigue</sym>, <sym>sleep disturbance</sym>, and <sym>psychomotor agitation</sym> related to anxiety. Symptom onset within 4 weeks postpartum aligns with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Urgent same-day referral to perinatal mental-health team or psychiatrist
2. Safety planning session now; remove or secure potential means of self-harm
3. Arrange support person to stay with her until professional review
4. Encourage 15-20 min outdoor daylight walks with baby to aid sleep-wake cycle
5. Offer crisis hotline numbers (e.g., 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, Postpartum Support International 1-800-944-4773)
6. Schedule follow-up call within 24 hrs to reassess mood and safety
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Screening Note – Postpartum Depression/Anxiety Screen

Presenting symptoms  
- Marked anhedonia and loss of anticipatory enjoyment  
- Daily low mood with tearfulness and emotional lability  
- Excessive self-blame/guilt re parenting competence  
- Persistent intrusive worry, nocturnal rumination, panic‐like episodes  
- Sleep initiation/maintenance difficulties tied to anxious rumination  
- Frequent feeling overwhelmed and unable to cope with routine tasks  

Pattern  
Symptoms present most days × ≥1 week, causing subjective distress and functional difficulty.

Significance  
Responses consistent with moderate–severe postpartum depressive and anxiety symptoms; meet threshold for further evaluation.

Safety  
Endorsed passive self-harm ideation (fleeting images, no plan/intent). → Acute safety concern; requires immediate risk assessment.

Recommendation  
Urgent referral to obstetric/maternal mental health team for comprehensive evaluation, safety planning, and discussion of treatment options.
